newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch borrowers chase cheap funds in Euromarkets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch borrowers chase cheap funds in Euromarkets.

text.p: Dutch companies are becoming more active borrowers on the Euromarkets as low interest rates tempt them to raise funds from yield-hungry institutions eager to invest their growing cash-piles.
Five Dutch companies have tapped the market to raise 2.0 billion guilders ($1.19 billion) through Eurobond issues in less than a week and bankers said more companies were expected to join them.
These issues bring to more than 33 billion guilders the amount raised through guilder-denominated Eurobonds so far in 1996, surpassing the 26.5 billion guilders raised in 1995.
A spokesman for retailer Ahold, which issued a 500 million guilder Eurobond on Monday, said it took advantage of the recent fall in Dutch interest rates to refinance debt.
Ahold assumed almost $1 billion of debt in its takeover of U.S. group Stop and Shop this year. "We are refinancing some of the debt because of the situation in the market," he said.

The 10-year Ahold issue was priced at 35 basis points over the government yield curve. Other recent issues, from mortgage bank Achmea Hypothekenebank, publisher Wolters Kluwer, copier firm Oce van der Grinten and ABN AMRO, were issued at spreads of 26-56 basis points.
Yields on 10-year Dutch state loans are now below 5.80 percent, the lowest level since January this year and more than 100 basis points below where they stood in June.
The absence of the Dutch government from the capital markets for the rest of this year and possibly part of next year has contributed to the bullish sentiment.
One fund manager said institutional investors were looking for ways to enhance their portfolios ahead of the year-end.
"They're scrambling for yield," he said.
A syndication manager said Dutch institutions were becoming more aware that corporate bonds could enhance their returns.
"Until now, they didn't have the staff or the energy to look at corporates. Now they're setting up desks to look at corporates to increase returns on their investments," he said.
He said Dutch fund managers were also placing more emphasis on their performance in relation to benchmark portfolios, which are usually government bonds.
With government bond yields so low, they were reluctant to invest more in state loans, increasing the liquidity of funds as their cash balances increased.
"That means there's a lot of cash around," the syndication manager said.
This turned the spotlight instead to so-called "spread products", higher-yielding corporate bonds which were being snapped up with relish by Dutch institutions.
But Euromarkets were only favourable for borrowers seeking fixed-rate debt as opportunities to swap into floating rate debt at favourable rates were not currently available, he said.
One debt originations manager said that in the last 10 years Dutch rates had rarely been as low as they are now.
"Absolute levels in Holland are becoming attractive for borrowers. For certain corporates it seems to be attractive to lock-in some long-term money," he said.
"I think we will probably see more deals," he added.
Chemicals group DSM has declined comment on talk that it plans its first Eurobond in five years.
The debt manager said most Dutch institutions were natural buyers of 10-year paper, the maturity of most recent issues.

With the Dutch yield curve so steep, fund managers could not afford to leave their funds as cash. "You have to look at longer maturities," he said, adding that although guilder yields may not drop much in the near future, corporate issues still offered a yield pick-up over state debt.
Another originations manager said the three major Dutch players in the guilder Eurobond market had been busy trying to convince Dutch companies to tap the market.

He said competition between these investment banks, ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, ING Barings and Rabobank was increasing as the end of the year approached and they tried to boost their position in Eurobond lead manager league tables.
"As a result, most of the issues you have seen are quite tight and expensive (to investors)," he said. ($1=1.688 Guilder)
